But what a depressingly large number of economists don't understand is that exchange rate adjustments do alter the saving/investment balance. They effectively shift income between consumers of tradable goods and producers of tradable goods. An appreciation, for example, puts downward pressure on saving by shifting income from net producers (e.g. manufacturers) to net consumers (the household sector), thereby rasing the consumption share of GDP.

In his 2008 paper, “The Real Exchange Rate and Economic Growth”, Dani Rodrik makes this point, arguing that a real depreciation is equivalent to a production subsidy plus a consumption tax on tradables. He then says that directly subsidizing tradable production would achieve the production-supporting effect without the consumption-tax effect.

And it's not just Rodrik. Almost everybody used to know this. In his 1944 book, Ragnar Nurkse said that “the devaluation of a currency is expansionary in effect if it corrects a previous overvaluation, but deflationary if it makes the currency undervalued.” He was making the same argument -- if saving is too low, devaluation expands production, and if it is too high, it weakens production.

Perhaps most famously, in his classic 1965 work on Argentina, Carlos Díaz Alejandro emphasized the redistribution caused by devaluation. A devaluation raises the domestic prices of tradable goods, reducing the real purchasing power of workers and consumers while benefiting producers and exporters. Because different groups have different propensities to consume and save, he explained, the redistribution can have major effects on aggregate demand and saving.

Peter Montiel in 2000 and Montiel and Servén in 2008 said the same thing, arguing that an undervalued currency changes intertemporal relative prices, discouraging consumption in favor of saving and making investment in tradables relatively more attractive than investment in non-tradables. Consequently, when the currency eventually appreciates, consumption rises and investment shifts toward non-tradables.

This is hardly a new idea. More generally, the distinction between policies that are intended to change an external imbalance and policies that are intended to change an internal imbalance is a spurious one. You cannot change one without the other, and either policy works by changing the saving/investment balance.

We seem to be seeing the acceleration of a 10-15 year trend in which economic activity increasingly shifts from the hard-budget constrained parts of the economy (for which the private sector is a rough proxy) to soft-budget constrained parts.

János Kornai's central insight was that a soft budget constraint changes behavior precisely because firms no longer have to treat losses as a binding signal. If an enterprise expects that the government will ultimately refinance or rescue it, the relationship between expenditure and expected return is undermined.

The result, Kornai argued, is likely to be a rising debt burden, excessive investment, weak price responsiveness,  and rising inefficiency.

“Chinamaxxing” isn’t simply a story about China becoming more effective at attracting young Westerners.

It is also a story about the West becoming more effective at alienating them.

This WSJ Opinion piece unintentionally illustrates an important reason why—ironically, through a mistake the author himself commits:

Growing distrust of Western media coverage of China, driven in part by cartoonishly biased framing not only of China’s achievements and progress.

Even the Chinamaxxing kids themselves are labeled “socialists”—because capitalists are apparently incapable of being impressed by cities like Shenzhen or Chinese EVs?

The fact is, young western people are not simply being pulled toward China by a relentless stream of images showing extraordinary advances in infrastructure, technology, manufacturing, robotics, EVs, and urban development.

They are also being pushed away from us by coverage that too often seems incapable of acknowledging those achievements without immediately reframing them as propaganda, manipulation, or some form of Chinese influence operation.

Consider this passage:

“TikTok abounds with footage of the fruits of China’s industrial might: gleaming neon metropolises, spotless subways, high-speed rail, humanoid robots, cutting-edge factories and hyper-‘efficient’ data centers. Millions of ‘Chinamaxxing’ Americans drool over what is sometimes known as ‘infrastructure porn’. It’s a subculture fueled by China’s relentless campaign to increase its soft power and flex its technological muscles for the benefit of its rivals.” @WSJopinion

Why reflexively reduce China’s very real achievements in technology, infrastructure, and modernization to the product of a Chinese soft-power campaign?

Why can’t those achievements also be recognized as extraordinarily impressive, highly consequential, and understandably capable of capturing the imagination of young people in the United States and around the world?

More importantly, why can’t they be highly motivating to the West’s own efforts to improve our competitive position vis-à-vis China?

That is what serious competitors do: study what their rivals do well, assess it objectively, learn from it, acquire capabilities from them where possible, and emerge more competitive as a result.

Need more persuasion? That is also exactly what China did.

The Owl View 🦉:

The more cartoonishly we portray China—and the more we caricature those who acknowledge its accomplishments—the wider the credibility gap becomes.

And the wider that gap becomes, the more we inadvertently strengthen the very phenomenon we are trying to explain.

Young people can see the gap for themselves.

A woman invested one hundred fifty thousand dollars from her personal retirement funds so that senior women would have access to reasonably priced housing and avoid spending their later years in solitude.

In the town of Cumby, Texas, seventy-year-old Robyn Yerian withdrew resources from her 401(k) account to establish The Bird’s Nest, a collection of compact residences designed expressly for older women who wanted both low-cost living arrangements and the company of others.

Across a five-acre property, Robyn arranged for essential services and prepared fourteen plots suitable for tiny homes. At present, eleven women ranging in age from sixty to eighty reside there, each contributing roughly four hundred fifty dollars monthly.

The residents discovered benefits that extended well beyond modest rental costs.

They prepare and enjoy meals together, assist with daily tasks, monitor one another’s health during periods of sickness, and gather beneath a shared outdoor structure. The setting has evolved into an environment in which advancing age need not equate to social isolation.

Interest in the community has been substantial. Robyn is said to have obtained over five hundred inquiries for the limited fourteen available positions.

She might have devoted her entire retirement nest egg exclusively to her own needs. Instead, she directed a portion of those savings toward creating an asset that many seniors value as highly as shelter itself: a neighborhood in which no individual is required to grow old in isolation.
